title: Distinguish router.refresh from server data invalidation
businessContext: Review a focused Next.js application change before it reaches production. The proposed file below contains the defect or unsupported assumption; external application services, where imported, are integration boundaries.
problemStatement: Review the proposed app/refresh-button.tsx change. Identify the incorrect framework assumption, propose a minimal corrected implementation, and provide evidence for the selected version scope and its 15/16 differences. Explain the interview variation after solving the base task. This is a framework code review: actual rendering, routing and cache behavior must be checked in a real Next.js build, not a browser function sandbox.
starterCode:
'use client';
export default function Refresh(){return <button onClick={()=>location.reload()}>Clear every cache</button>;}

constraints: Preserve the stated user behavior and keep trust boundaries explicit.
Use the selected version’s documented API; do not suppress build/type failures to hide the defect.

Repeat while its public data remains cached.
Invalidate the assigned data tag at the mutation boundary and compare the next refresh.

alternativeApproaches: It targets a path/layout’s cached route behavior in an allowed server context. Shared data used by other routes may need tag-based invalidation too; write down the read graph before choosing the smallest correct invalidation scope.
commonMistakes: Verifying only next dev when the behavior depends on production rendering or bundling.
Treating a visible UI state, matcher or TypeScript type as a substitute for server-side validation and authorization.
